subject: Canada hiked rates, then lost 4,700 jobs
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a variable mortgage or a renewal coming up in the next year, the two numbers that set your payment moved in opposite directions over the past ten days. The Bank of Canada raised rates on October 28, and on Friday Statistics Canada said the country lost jobs in October.

## A hike built on oil

BNN Bloomberg reported on October 28 that the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, the first increase since July 2023. CBC reported the same day that Governor Tiff Macklem said the move was needed in the face of persistent inflation. His case was narrow and specific. Oil prices and refinery margins have stayed high, CPI inflation has sat near 3 per cent since April, and the Bank expects it to reach roughly 3.5 per cent by year end. Macklem said the increase was meant to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill over and turn into generalized inflation. He also said Governing Council would take future decisions one meeting at a time, which is central banker for we are committing to nothing. Markets had expected the hike, and Bloomberg reported it was the consensus of Bay Street economists in its survey.

## Friday's jobs report went the other way

Statistics Canada released the October Labour Force Survey on Friday, and it reads worse the longer you look at it. Employment fell by 4,700 against a consensus call for a gain of about 13,600. The unemployment rate rose to 6.7 per cent from 6.5. Underneath the headline, full-time work dropped by 18,100 and private sector employment fell by 52,500, according to TD Economics. Youth unemployment climbed 0.7 points to 13.7 per cent. Ontario and Alberta both sit at 7.3 per cent now. The wage line is the one I would stare at. Average hourly wages rose 2.2 per cent year over year, down from 2.3 per cent in September, which is below the rate of inflation. Workers are not the ones pushing prices up. TD's Andrew Hencic said ongoing labour force growth means there is growing slack in the labour market.

## The split the Bank has to resolve by December 9

Here is the tension I cannot get past. The Bank is raising rates to fight an oil shock. The economy is not running hot. **Core inflation**, the measures that strip out the most volatile prices to show the underlying trend, is still close to 2 per cent. September's headline figure of 3.1 per cent came with gasoline up 27.8 per cent year over year and inflation excluding gasoline at 2.2 per cent. Rate hikes do not drill oil wells. What they do is slow hiring and squeeze borrowers, in a country that has now shed jobs for three months running by TD's count. The Bank's stated worry is pass-through, meaning firms that have absorbed higher input costs so far will start charging customers instead. That is a reasonable fear. A labour market at 6.7 per cent unemployment with 2.2 per cent wage growth is a strange place for it to begin.

## The takeaway

I think December 9 is a hold, and markets moved my way on Friday, with TD Economics noting that pricing for a January hike slid to 77 per cent from 96 per cent the day before the report. Watch the October CPI on November 16 at 8:30 Eastern. If headline inflation prints near 3.5 per cent while core sits at 2, Macklem has a much harder sell to his own Governing Council. If you are renewing a mortgage inside the next six months, take a rate hold now instead of betting on cuts that are not on anybody's calendar.
